title: Sole Meunière
subtitle: Sole fillets in a browned butter and lemon sauce
excerpt: The most famous way to cook sole: fillets dusted in flour and fried briefly in clarified butter, finished with a beurre noisette of whole butter cooked until nutty-brown and sharpened with lemon. Done in five minutes, ready to serve.

recipe.sourceNotes: Sole meunière (meunière means the miller's wife, referring to the dusting of flour) is one of the great classic French preparations for flat fish, and particularly associated with the sole from the North Sea and English Channel, which has been prized by French cooks since at least the seventeenth century. Julia Child described her first experience of sole meunière at a Rouen restaurant in 1948 as a culinary epiphany that changed her life and directly inspired her career. The dish is the simplest possible expression of good fish cookery: the best fish, the best butter, lemon, and nothing more. Dover sole is the classic choice for its dense, sweet flesh and elegant flat bone structure; lemon sole is more available and cheaper but slightly less firm.

content.text: The pan must be very hot before the fish goes in: sole fillets cook in 2 minutes per side and the pan must maintain that temperature throughout. Pat the fillets dry and flour them just before cooking; flour left on fish too long becomes gummy. The beurre noisette is made in the same pan after the fish is removed: add cold butter and let it foam and turn brown before adding the lemon, which will spit and splutter. Work quickly.

items.preparation: large fillets, skin on or off; patted very dry
40 g for frying, 40 g for the beurre noisette
to prevent the butter burning during frying

content.text: Season the sole fillets with salt and pepper. Dust lightly on both sides with the seasoned flour, shaking off any excess. Heat a large frying pan over high heat. Add 40 g of butter and the oil. When the butter is foaming and just starting to colour, add the sole fillets.

Cook the fillets for 1.5 to 2 minutes until golden on the underside. Turn carefully and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more: the fish is done when it is opaque throughout and the flesh flakes easily when pressed. Transfer to warmed plates.

Add the remaining 40 g of cold butter to the same pan. Cook over medium-high heat, swirling the pan, until the butter turns a deep golden-brown and smells nutty. Add the lemon juice (it will spit), swirl once, and immediately pour the beurre noisette over the fish. Scatter with parsley and serve at once.
